Herald decides whether a message is worth interrupting you for before a word of it is said. Each message carries an importance, the page sets a floor, and the engine returns a verdict.

We sent one at 80 against a floor of 50 and it was delivered: the 3D character in the corner of the page said it. We sent the next at 29. The character said nothing, and the verdict came back as a drop with its reason: below-importance-floor.

Every message that is not delivered comes back with a reason, so why you were not told has an answer.

A drop and a hold are different verdicts.

A held message is delivered once the thing blocking it clears: another message on screen, a tab in the background, a full rate limit, quiet hours. A dropped one is reported with its reason and will not be delivered.
A verdict of deliver is what makes the 3D character speak, with the gesture the sender chose. On a page with no GPU the same verdict arrives as a card, in a live region, dismissible with Escape.

In the reel, two different characters: the verdict is breaking, with 2 joints lost, 5 animations removed and 4 objects renamed rather than rewritten. three.ws/diff

Severity is one of none, cosmetic, minor, major, breaking, so a build can gate on it. Breaking means something a consumer references by name is gone: a clip, a joint, a mesh. That is the failure that renders fine and never moves.

Vertex data is compared at a quantum of 1e-4 units, so the float drift of a re-export does not register while a genuine edit does.

The same engine runs this page, the CLI and the free API, so a verdict in CI cannot disagree with what you see here. Hand the CLI two files and a --fail-on level, and the build fails on the severity you choose.

A nine-cylinder radial engine and a steam locomotive, with no model file behind either one. It is a Labs experiment in building 3D geometry from code instead of files.

Both machines are built when the page loads: dimensions become profiles, profiles get revolved or extruded, and the results are merged into the parts you can see. The motion is solved, not baked animation. Pistons come from the exact planar slider-crank, and the locomotive valve gear closes a four-bar chain by intersecting circles every frame, which is why a rod length that cannot physically reach refuses to move rather than stretching.

Each machine is a small JSON object of numbers. Copy the spec, hand it to an agent, get a different machine back, then export the result as GLB. three.ws/assembly

posts.text:
Every point on three.ws/globe is open data, and it links back to its source. Conflict, force posture and sanctions are classified from a global news event stream and held in a rolling window, so the time control is real: switching from 7 days to 30 took the map from more than 1,000 points to more than 5,000.

Eleven layers on one globe: conflict, force posture, sanctions, natural events, severe weather, internet outages and economic stress, over military bases, nuclear sites and maritime choke points. None of it needs a key.

Natural events come from the US Geological Survey and NASA, severe weather from the Global Disaster Alert and Coordination System, internet outages from Georgia Tech, and economic stress from World Bank indicators. Ask for more time than the rolling window holds and the layer tells you how much it actually covered, rather than padding the rest.

Standard parts come from bd_warehouse: involute spur gears, ISO threads, nuts, cap screws, washers and ball bearings. The Python runs anywhere after pip install build123d bd_warehouse.

posts.text: A glTF file, Three.js and WebGL on the viewer's own GPU. No plugin, no video stream, no server drawing frames. Here is the full path of one rigged character, from a sentence to a lit, animated model in a browser tab, in six stages.

posts.text: To start, make. The Forge turns text or an image into a mesh with open models running on our own Cloud Run GPUs: TRELLIS, Hunyuan3D and TripoSG. Draft is about 12,000 polygons, Standard about 30,000 with 2K textures, High up to 200,000 polygons with full PBR.

Next, pack and load. The file is compressed for the wire, then the browser decodes it with Draco, KTX2 and meshopt through GLTFLoader, using same-origin decoders loaded on demand. The free validator checks the result against the Khronos suite, in your browser.

media.alt: The three.ws glTF validator page reporting the result of a Khronos validation run in the browser

posts.text: Then light. Lighting from a PMREM environment map, a three-point rig and Khronos PBR-Neutral tone mapping, so colours stay true to the material. Holo Sticker turns the same lit model into a shareable card.

media.alt: The three.ws Holo Sticker page showing a lit 3D character rendered live in the browser

posts.text: Then motion. A canonicalizer maps the bone names of Mixamo, VRM, Unreal, Rigify, Daz and more to one set, so a single clip library drives any humanoid. Faces move through ARKit morph targets with nine-viseme lip sync. Pose Studio lets you keyframe your own.

posts.text: Last, embed. One script tag and one element put the character on any website. Rig Doctor, free and in your browser, tells you before you start whether your own avatar will animate.
